newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran in final hours of election campaign.
newsitem.headline: Iran in final hours of election campaign.

text.p: Iran's presidential candidates launched their final campaign efforts on Wednesday with conflicting opinion polls unable to agree on a clear likely winner in Friday's election.
The Islamic republic's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said at a religious gathering in Tehran the election was a divine test for the nation.
"Excitement and liveliness flood the country...this is exactly what we begged of God and what our enemies did not want. They wanted people to ignore the elections," he said.
Khamenei said a large turnout in the election would be "a smack in the mouth of the enemy".
He appealed for calm and said there were signs of the enemy's hand playing tricks in Iran and fabricating rumours about the possibility of vote-rigging.
"Personally, I won't allow the election to be unhealthy. The president will be a legal one," he added.

A nationwide poll by group of centrists and technocrats backing Mohammad Khatami published in Akhbar newspaper gave the former culture and Islamic guidance minister 59 percent of popular support with 30 percent for his main rival, parliament speaker Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri. It gave the two other candidates the remaining 11 percent.
A poll published on Tuesday showed the reverse result with a clear lead for Nateq-Nouri.
Both men are Shi'ite Moslem clergymen.
If Nateq-Nouri gains the presidency revolutionary Iran's veteran Foreign Minister Ali Akbar Velayati is likely to be his vice-president, Iranian analysts said.

Velayati, a soft-spoken university professor trained as a paediatrician, has publicly endorsed the speaker. He could keep the foreign affairs portfolio which has made him the voice of the Islamic republic in world capitals over the last 17 years.
The presidency is Iran's highest elective office but second in authority to the supreme leader. The post of prime minister was abolished in 1989.
Campaigning ends at midnight (1930 GMT), allowing one day for rest and reflection before voting on Friday. The result is not expected to emerge before Monday.

Election officials and President Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who must step down in August after two consecutive four-year terms in office, have warned against violations and 280 people have been detained for unspecified offences in the capital.
Rafsanjani has cautioned government officials against abusing their position to influence the election and said vote-rigging would be an unforgivable treason.

The head of the Guardian Council, a powerful body of 12 clerics and lawyers which selected four presidential candidates from a field of 238 on the basis of their belief in the Islamic system of government, said any violations of election rules must be countered without discrimination.

Interior Ministry inspectors will supervise the election but no international observers have been invited and vote counting will be done behind closed doors. Candidates or their representatives will not be allowed to witness the count.
Some 33 million Iranians aged 15 and over can vote.
Nateq-Nouri is widely tipped to win.

"Rafsanjani was speaker before he became president so Nateq-Nouri is almost designated to take over," said one of the few Western diplomats left in Tehran after Iran's recent row with the European Union over allegations of complicity in political assassinations of Kurdish dissidents in Germany.
Rafsanjani will continue to wield influence in Iran as head of the Expediency Council, a body which mediates any dispute between the parliament and the Guardian Council.
